name: Parvati
definition: Parvati is a composite portrait of a Scheduled Caste woman in Yadgir district, navigating the daily pressures of wage labour, water scarcity and her children's schooling in Karnataka's lowest-literacy district. She embodies the lived realities of the region's Article 371(J) promise alongside persistent poverty, drought and seasonal migration.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Parvati wakes before dawn to fetch water from the hand-pump two lanes away, filling three brass pots before the queue lengthens. She works as a domestic helper in three households in Surpur town, sweeping, washing vessels and clothes, earning around four thousand rupees a month. During the cotton-picking and tur-harvest seasons she joins gangs of labourers on surrounding farms, earning a daily wage of two hundred and fifty to three hundred rupees when work is available. Her husband drives an auto-rickshaw on the Surpur-Yadgir route but income is irregular, especially in the summer months when diesel costs rise and passengers are fewer. The household survives on her combined earnings, his occasional fares, MGNREGA work when the gram panchayat sanctions it, and the ten kilos of subsidised rice they collect under Anna Bhagya each month. Parvati budgets every rupee: milk for the children, vegetables twice a week, kerosene for the stove, mobile recharge to stay in touch with her sister who migrated to Hyderabad years ago. Drought years mean fewer farm-labour days and deeper debt to the town's small moneylender, whose interest she pays monthly without touching the principal.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Parvati lives with her husband, her mother-in-law, her thirteen-year-old daughter Kaveri and ten-year-old son Raju in a two-room house on the edge of Surpur town. Her husband's younger brother left for construction work in Bengaluru five years ago and sends money irregularly. Her mother-in-law, now frail and partially blind, mostly stays home minding the house and preparing the afternoon meal of jowar rotti and chutney. Parvati was married at sixteen, soon after she stopped attending school in Class Seven; her own schooling ended when her parents could not afford the bus fare to the high school in the next village. She hopes her daughter will finish at least SSLC. Kaveri now studies in Class Eight at the government high school in Surpur town, travelling by the morning KKRTC bus under the Shakti scheme, which costs the family nothing. Raju attends the Urdu-medium primary school near their lane. Parvati's days are shaped by the double burden of paid work and all household tasks: cooking, washing, fetching water, and caring for her mother-in-law. Her husband helps occasionally but sees domestic work as her domain. Gender roles are firmly set and Parvati negotiates them quietly, knowing that open argument brings trouble.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Parvati studied in the village government Kannada school until Class Seven, learning to read and write but leaving before she could appear for the high school entrance. She still regrets not finishing, feeling the gap every time she needs to read a government notice or help Kaveri with homework. Kaveri now attends the government girls' high school in Surpur town, a four-kilometre ride on the KKRTC bus each morning under the Shakti free-travel scheme, which removed the single biggest expense that would have forced Parvati to pull her daughter out. The school charges no fees under the Right to Education Act but there are hidden costs: notebooks, pens, the annual thirty-rupee exam fee, the grey uniform skirt and white blouse that must be bought new each year as Kaveri grows. Raju studies at the local Urdu-medium school because it is closer and several neighbours' children go there; Parvati worries he will struggle later if he needs to switch to Kannada-medium high school. She dreams that Kaveri will pass SSLC, perhaps even study further and find a government job under the Article 371(J) reservation, though she does not fully understand how the system works. The school headmistress once mentioned scholarships for SC students and Parvati means to ask again, but the paperwork intimidates her and she has no time to chase it during the day.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Parvati's own health is worn down by years of hard labour and poor nutrition. She suffers from chronic joint pain in her knees and lower back, likely worsened by carrying heavy water pots and bending over cotton rows, but she has never taken a full day's rest or consulted a doctor about it. When pain flares she buys a strip of paracetamol from the shop near the bus stand. Her mother-in-law's eyesight has dimmed with age and untreated cataracts; the family was told at the Primary Health Centre that free surgery is available at the district hospital in Yadgir town under a government scheme, but arranging the trip, the escort and the days off work has proven impossible so far. Kaveri and Raju have been given routine vaccinations and deworming tablets at school. Parvati worries about the well water and hand-pump water in Surpur, which sometimes tastes bitter and leaves a white stain on vessels; she has heard talk of fluoride in the groundwater and seen a few older people in the area with bent backs and stained teeth, though no official has come to test their water or explain the risk. The 108 ambulance service is known and once took a neighbour's child to Yadgir during a fever emergency, but Parvati prays she will never need it. She relies on the anganwadi for basic advice and the government hospital in Surpur for fevers and minor complaints, knowing that anything serious means a costly trip to Kalaburagi or Raichur.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Parvati belongs to the Madiga community, one of the region's largest Scheduled Caste groups, whose traditional leather-work occupation her family left behind a generation ago in search of less stigmatised wage labour. The Madiga colony sits at the edge of Surpur town, a cluster of thirty-odd households that share water pumps, a small neighbourhood temple to Yellamma and a collective memory of caste insult and exclusion. Parvati and her family worship Yellamma and also visit the Hanuman temple in the town centre during festivals, though she is conscious of the subtle caste distance maintained by some upper-caste townspeople. Her husband and several neighbours are members of the Ambedkar Sangha, which occasionally organises meetings and community meals on Ambedkar Jayanti. Parvati draws strength from the company of other women in the colony who work similar jobs and share similar struggles; they gather in the evenings to chat, exchange news and sometimes collectively confront an employer who withholds wages. The Shakti bus scheme has given her new mobility and a sense that the government occasionally notices people like her. She speaks Kannada at home and at work, though she understands a little Urdu from her son's schoolmates and the town's Muslim shopkeepers. Religion and caste shape her daily interactions, but she tries to shield her children from the worst of it, hoping education and a government job might give them a different life.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Parvati interacts with the government mainly through ration-card collection at the fair-price shop, where she receives ten kilos of rice and two kilos of sugar each month under Anna Bhagya, and through MGNREGA job cards that her husband holds for both of them. Work under MGNREGA is irregular; the gram panchayat sanctions it in short bursts for road repair or tank desilting, and wages often arrive months late in their bank account. She has heard of Article 371(J) and the special status for Kalyana Karnataka but does not fully understand what it means for her family, beyond a vague promise of local jobs and reservations that educated people might access. The Shakti free-bus scheme is the government benefit she feels most directly: it has kept Kaveri in school by removing the daily travel cost. She has never attended a gram sabha meeting; such spaces feel remote and male-dominated, and her working hours leave no time. Officials and local leaders rarely visit the colony except at election time. When a government health worker came last year to register families for Ayushman Bharat cards, Parvati gave her details but has not received the card yet and does not know whom to ask. The state feels distant, occasionally helpful through schemes like Shakti and Anna Bhagya, but mostly indifferent to daily struggles like water scarcity, wage theft and her mother-in-law's untreated cataracts.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Parvati worries constantly about money: whether the month's earnings will cover rice, vegetables, school costs and the moneylender's interest payment. She worries about water, especially in summer when the hand-pump runs dry by mid-morning and she must walk further to the borewell near the highway. She worries about Raju's future, knowing that boys without education end up as daily labourers or auto-drivers like his father, trapped in the same cycle. Parvati is proud that she has kept both children in school so far, longer than her own parents managed for her, and proud of Kaveri's report card and the teacher's praise. She blames the lack of jobs, the drought and the cost of everything for the hardship her family faces, and she blames caste prejudice for the small humiliations and wage discrimination she encounters. She does not blame herself or her children. She demands water supply in the colony, regular MGNREGA work at fair wages paid on time, and a government that remembers Yadgir district exists. She has heard officials call Yadgir the most backward district in Karnataka and while the label angers her—because it sounds like blame—she also uses it to argue that the government owes her family more. She wants Kaveri to finish school, find a government job and escape the life of domestic and farm labour. She knows the odds are against them but she works every day toward that hope, carrying water, washing dishes, picking cotton, and counting every rupee.
